ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: NLRP3 inflammasome activation requires both transcriptional priming and complex assembly, but how RNA m6A methylation coordinates these steps remains unclear. Here, we show that m6A levels increase during macrophage NLRP3 inflammasome activation and that METTL3 loss suppresses this activation. Myeloid-specific Mettl3 knockout mice display reduced inflammation and improved metabolic outcomes in lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced sepsis, monosodium urate (MSU)-induced arthritis, and diet-induced obesity. Integrated chromatin-associated RNA sequencing (chrRNA-seq), kethoxal-assisted single-stranded DNA sequencing (KAS-seq), and chrRNA-methylated RNA immunoprecipitation (MeRIP)-seq analyses show that METTL3 installs m6A co-transcriptionally on nascent Jak1, Nlrp3, and Il1β RNAs and that METTL3 regulates dynamic transcription and chromatin accessibility while selectively maintaining Nlrp3/Il1β transcription. YTHDF1-driven translation of Jak1 activates the JAK1-STAT3-C/EBPβ axis to initiate Nlrp3/Il1β transcription, and m6A-YTHDF1 translation of Nlrp3/Il1β amplifies protein output, forming a coupled transcriptional-translational circuit. Pharmacologic STAT3 inhibition and METTL3 catalytic rescue validate this pathway and identify METTL3-mediated m6A as a therapeutic target for inflammasome-driven diseases.

ce:section.ce:para: Inflammasomes represent a unique category of multiprotein complexes known for their pivotal role in the innate immune response to pathogenic invasions and tissue damage.1,2,3,4 A classic inflammasome comprises pattern recognition receptors, the effector protein caspase-1, and the scaffold apoptosis-associated speck-like protein containing a CARD (ASC).5,6 Upon activation, these pattern recognition receptors form polymers and subsequently recruit ASC and pro-caspase-1 to assemble into the inflammasome, ultimately activating caspase-1.7,8 Once activated, caspase-1 serves a dual function. Firstly, it cleaves proinflammatory cytokines IL-1β and IL-18 precursors, promoting their maturation and subsequent release. Secondly, activated caspase-1 cleaves GSDMD, releasing its N-terminal active segment.9 This active segment punctures holes in the cell membrane, triggering cell death known as “pyroptosis.”10,11 NLRP3 inflammasome is the best-studied inflammasome, and its excessive activation relates to autoimmune diseases and inflammatory diseases.

N6-methyladenosine (m6A) is the most abundant internal modification in eukaryotic mRNA.12,13,14,15 In recent years, it has been shown to broadly regulate NLRP3 inflammasome activity at the post-transcriptional level.16,17,18,19 For example, in acute kidney injury, IGF2BP1 recognizes the m6A site of E2f1 mRNA, stabilizes its expression, increases MIF levels, and induces NLRP3-related pyroptosis.20 Betaine promotes YTHDF2-mediated degradation of Nlrp3 mRNA, thereby suppressing microglial NLRP3 activation.21 Lactate-induced ALKBH5 demethylation reduces Nlrp3 mRNA stability.22 Meanwhile, WTAP and METTL14 enhance Nlrp3 mRNA stability through m6A modification, aggravating inflammation.23,24 YTHDF1 facilitates the translation of CLOCK and amplifies the NLRP3 signaling pathway through liquid-liquid phase separation.25 Collectively, these studies indicate that the m6A “writer-reader-eraser” axis profoundly influences NLRP3 activity in multiple pathological contexts through post-transcriptional regulation. However, it remains unclear whether, during macrophage NLRP3 inflammasome activation, m6A also acts in a co-transcriptional manner to regulate chromatin remodeling and nascent RNA transcription, and how the m6A marks on nascent RNA are recognized to initiate transcription of inflammasome-related genes. Although previous studies have suggested that METTL3 can influence chromatin states, bind promoter elements, and install m6A marks on nascent RNA to directly regulate transcription,26,27,28,29,30 it is still unknown whether and how these mechanisms function during macrophage inflammasome activation. Our study focuses on addressing this question.

In this work, we combined chromatin-associated RNA sequencing (chrRNA-seq), chrRNA-MeRIP-seq, kethoxal-assisted single-stranded DNA sequencing (KAS-seq), polysome profiling, RNA-FISH (fluorescence in situ hybridization) colocalization, and rescue experiments to build an integrated chromatin-transcription-translation map of macrophages during NLRP3 inflammasome activation. We found that, upon inflammatory stimulation, METTL3 installs m6A marks on nascent RNA, particularly on Jak1, Nlrp3, and Il1β transcripts. Among them, the m6A modification on Jak1 is recognized by YTHDF1, which enhances its polysome loading and translation, thereby activating the JAK1-STAT3 pathway and driving C/EBPβ-mediated transcription of Nlrp3 and Il1β. In parallel, m6A-YTHDF1 directly promotes the translation of Nlrp3 and Il1β mRNAs, further amplifying protein production after transcription initiation. Notably, METTL3 deletion increases global chromatin accessibility and relieves widespread transcriptional repression but selectively reduces the transcription of Nlrp3 and Il1β. We interpret this “decoupling” phenomenon using a hierarchical model: under inflammatory stimulation, the METTL3-m6A axis regulates global transcriptional activity, while the selective decrease in Nlrp3/Il1β transcription arises from insufficient m6A-dependent JAK1-STAT3-C/EBPβ signaling, which directly determines whether these genes are effectively transcribed. Finally, in myeloid-specific Mettl3 conditional knockout mice and STAT3 inhibitor-treated mice, we confirmed that the METTL3-m6A-JAK1-STAT3-C/EBPβ axis critically controls NLRP3 inflammasome-mediated inflammation in vivo, as demonstrated in models of sepsis, MSU-induced arthritis, and obesity-related chronic inflammation.

ce:section.ce:section-title: METTL3-mediated m6A methylation promotes NLRP3 inflammasome activation in macrophages
ce:section.ce:para: To investigate the role of RNA m6A modification in macrophage NLRP3 inflammasome activation, we established NLRP3 inflammasome models in J774A.1 cells and bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMDMs). Consistent results from m6A immunofluorescence, mRNA m6A quantification by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS), and mRNA m6A dot blot analysis (Figures 1A–1D) showed that m6A modification was markedly increased following inflammasome activation. However, regardless of NLRP3 activation, the expression of m6A-related writer, eraser, and reader proteins showed no significant changes (Figures S1A–S1D), indicating that the elevated m6A level was not caused by altered expression of these enzymes. To identify the major methyltransferase responsible, we generated METTL3- and METTL14-deficient J774A.1 macrophages (Figures S2A–S2B) and quantified m6A levels. Under LPS + ATP stimulation, METTL3 deletion reduced global mRNA m6A levels by approximately 50%, whereas METTL14 deletion caused only about a 20% reduction (Figure S2C), suggesting that METTL3 is the dominant m6A writer in this context. Furthermore, in Nlrp3 knockout J774A.1 cells, LPS + ATP stimulation did not decrease global m6A levels, and the protein expression of METTL3, METTL14, and the demethylase FTO remained comparable to wild-type (WT) cells (Figures S3A–S3B). These findings indicate that the increase in m6A is independent of NLRP3 activation and more likely represents an upstream regulatory event rather than a downstream consequence.

At the functional level, we established two independent METTL3-deficient J774A.1 cell lines (sh-Mettl3 #1/#2) (Figure S2A). In the LPS + ATP model, METTL3 loss significantly reduced IL-1β secretion in the supernatant and decreased the cleavage of caspase-1 and GSDMD (Figures 1E and 1H). In addition, NLRP3 and pro-IL-1β protein levels were notably reduced, whereas pro-IL-18, pro-caspase-1, ASC, and full-length GSDMD were largely unaffected (Figure 1E). This inhibitory effect was also observed when NLRP3 was activated by other stimuli, including nigericin and MSU crystals (Figure 1K), resulting in decreased NLRP3 and pro-IL-1β expression, reduced caspase-1 cleavage, and lower IL-1β secretion. In primary macrophages, we crossed Mettl3f/f mice with Lyz2-Cre mice to generate myeloid-specific METTL3-deficient mice (Lyz2-Cre-Mettl3f/f) (Figure S4A). In both BMDMs and peritoneal macrophages (PMs) from these mice, METTL3 deletion similarly inhibited NLRP3 inflammasome activation and IL-1β secretion, consistent with the findings in cell lines (Figures 1F–1G and 1I–1J). ASC oligomerization and speck formation are key steps in inflammasome assembly. Under secondary stimulation, METTL3 deficiency markedly impaired ASC oligomerization and speck formation (Figures 1L–1N). As a downstream effect, activated caspase-1 cleaves GSDMD to release GSDMD-N, which forms pores in the plasma membrane and triggers pyroptosis. We assessed N-GSDMD accumulation in the membrane fraction and LDH release, and found that METTL3 loss significantly reduced both (Figures 1O–1P), suggesting that pyroptosis was suppressed and cell viability improved.

Taken together, METTL3 acts as a key positive regulator of NLRP3 inflammasome activation in macrophages. As the dominant m6A writer, METTL3 drives the global increase of m6A during inflammatory activation—independent of NLRP3 itself—while its deletion suppresses IL-1β secretion, caspase-1, and GSDMD cleavage, ASC oligomerization, and pyroptosis. These results collectively establish the central role of the METTL3-m6A axis in promoting macrophage NLRP3 inflammasome activation.

ce:section.ce:section-title: METTL3 enhances Il1β and Nlrp3 transcription through its catalytic m6A activity
ce:section.ce:para: Our previous results showed that METTL3 deficiency in macrophages markedly reduced NLRP3 and pro-IL-1β protein levels, but had little effect on pro-IL-18, pro–caspase-1, ASC, or full-length GSDMD (Figure 1E). To clarify the molecular mechanism underlying this regulation, we systematically examined how METTL3 affects the expression of inflammasome-related genes during NLRP3 activation. Under unstimulated conditions, loss of METTL3 did not alter the mRNA levels of inflammasome-related genes (Figure 2A). However, after LPS or LPS + ATP stimulation, the mRNA levels of Il1β and Nlrp3 were selectively decreased, while Caspase1, Asc, Il18, and Gsdmd remained unchanged (Figure 2B). To distinguish whether these effects were due to transcriptional or post-transcriptional regulation, we analyzed m6A modification and mRNA stability of Il1β and Nlrp3 transcripts during activation. Inflammasome activation markedly increased m6A modification on both transcripts in a METTL3-dependent manner (Figure 2C). However, actinomycin D chase assays revealed no significant difference in their half-lives between control and METTL3-deficient cells (Figure 2D). Furthermore, luciferase reporter assays driven by the Il1β and Nlrp3 promoters showed that METTL3 deficiency significantly reduced reporter activity upon LPS or LPS + ATP stimulation, indicating that the downregulation results from reduced transcriptional activity rather than altered mRNA stability (Figures 2E and 2F). To directly test whether METTL3 catalytic activity is required, we re-expressed either wild-type METTL3 or a catalytically inactive mutant (D395A) in sh-Mettl3 J774A.1 cells and in BMDMs from Lyz2-Cre-Mettl3f/f mice. In both systems, only wild-type METTL3—but not D395A—restored Il1β and Nlrp3 expression, while caspase-1 mRNA remained unaffected (Figures 2G–2I and S5B). These results demonstrate that METTL3 promotes Il1β and Nlrp3 expression in an m6A-dependent catalytic manner rather than through non-enzymatic structural functions. Subcellular fractionation and colocalization analyses further showed that METTL3 translocates from the nucleoplasm to the chromatin fraction upon inflammasome activation (Figure 2J) and colocalizes strongly with the nuclear speck marker SC-35 (Figure 2K), consistent with its role in co-transcriptional m6A deposition and transcriptional regulation. Notably, CUT&Tag profiling identified 839 METTL3-bound DNA fragments but showed no enrichment at the Il1β and Nlrp3 promoter regions nor at promoters of other core inflammasome genes (Figures 2L–2N). These data suggest that METTL3 does not directly occupy these promoters but instead enhances Il1β and Nlrp3 transcription indirectly through its m6A catalytic activity, acting on co-transcriptional or chromatin-associated RNAs.

Together, these findings indicate that METTL3 specifically promotes Il1β and Nlrp3 transcription during inflammatory activation through its m6A methyltransferase activity, while this effect is independent of mRNA stability changes.

ce:section.ce:section-title: METTL3 regulates global dynamic transcription and chromatin accessibility during macrophage NLRP3 inflammasome activation
ce:section.ce:para: To determine the role of METTL3 in genome-wide transcriptional regulation during NLRP3 inflammasome activation, we activated the inflammasome in sh-Scramble and sh-Mettl3 macrophages. Chromatin-associated RNA (chrRNA) was purified and analyzed by chrRNA-seq (Figure 3A). About half of the detected chrRNAs were intronic fragments (≈50%) (Figure 3B), indicating that they represent nascent and incompletely spliced transcripts. At the non-coding level, inflammasome activation changed the expression of 668 long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) (Figure S6A), while METTL3 loss had little effect on these changes (Figure S6B). Comparative analysis of the nascent transcriptome (coding RNA), inflammasome activation significantly altered the transcription of 1,325 genes (padj < 0.05, fold change > 2) (Figure 3C); METTL3 depletion caused 221 genes to change significantly (Figure 3D). Among them, nascent transcription of Nlrp3 and Il1β was selectively reduced (Figures 3D and 3E). In contrast, genes such as Asc, Gsdmd, Caspase1, Nek7, and Il18 were not affected (Figure 3D). Globally, inflammasome activation was accompanied by a broad decrease in nascent transcription (Figure 3F). When METTL3 was absent, this suppression was partially relieved (Figure 3F). Total RNA-seq results showed a similar trend (Figure 3G). 5-ethynyl uridine (EU)-Click-iT labeling confirmed that LPS and LPS+ATP inhibited nascent RNA synthesis (Figure 3H). METTL3 deficiency, however, significantly reduced this inhibition (Figure 3H). Cross-analysis showed that 37% of the downregulated genes in activated sh-Mettl3 cells were normally upregulated after activation in control cells (Figure 3I). These included key inflammatory genes such as Nlrp3 and Il1β. Together, these results indicate that METTL3 participates in the remodeling of global transcriptional activity during inflammasome activation. To test whether this effect depends on METTL3’s catalytic activity, we performed rescue experiments in sh-Mettl3 cells using either wild-type METTL3 or the catalytically inactive mutant D395A. Only METTL3-WT restored nuclear EU signals to near-baseline levels. The D395A mutant and empty vector had no effect. This “WT reversible, mutant ineffective” pattern supports that METTL3 reshapes nascent transcription through its m6A catalytic activity (Figure S6C). To further assess chromatin changes, we performed KAS-seq to measure genome-wide chromatin accessibility (Figure 3K). After inflammasome activation, METTL3-deficient cells showed a global increase in chromatin accessibility (Figures 3L–3N). The number of open promoter peaks increased from 2,275 to 3,199 (Figure 3O). Separate analyses of promoters and enhancers produced similar results (Figures S7A–S7B). Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis showed that these differential peaks were related to immune regulation, development, and transcriptional control (Figures 3P–3Q). At the gene level, METTL3 loss mainly altered chromatin accessibility at the Nlrp3 and Il1β loci (Figures 3R and 3S), while other inflammasome genes were largely unchanged. Combining chrRNA-seq and KAS-seq data, we conclude that METTL3 regulates global chromatin-transcription dynamics and selectively promotes Nlrp3 and Il1β transcription during inflammasome activation.

ce:section.ce:section-title: METTL3 promotes Nlrp3 and Il1β transcription by regulating the transcription factor C/EBPβ
ce:section.ce:para: While we have established that METTL3 controls the global dynamic transcription during macrophage NLRP3 inflammasome activation, it remains unclear why METTL3 specifically participates in regulating Nlrp3 and Il1β gene transcription. Many studies have explored the relationship between METTL3 and histones to regulate a series of gene expressions associated with specific phenotypes. However, given the specificity of METTL3’s impact on Nlrp3 and Il1β gene transcription during NLRP3 inflammasome activation, we believe that this specificity may not be related to histones but could be associated with specific transcription factors responsible for Nlrp3 and Il1β gene activation. Upon literature review, we found that the common transcription factors for Nlrp3 and Il1β genes include C/EBPβ and ZFP217 (Figure 4A). In nascent transcript data, we observed that METTL3 significantly inhibited the generation of C/ebpβ nascent transcripts while having no effect on Zfp217 (Figure 4B). Moreover, by analyzing KAS-seq data, we assessed the accessibility of the C/ebpβ and Zfp217 genes. Interestingly, we discovered that METTL3 deficiency significantly reduced the activity of the C/ebpβ gene promoter region while not affecting the transcription activity of Zfp217 (Figure 4C). Subsequently, through western blot experiments, we found that METTL3 markedly suppressed C/EBPβ protein expression (Figure 4D). Furthermore, we conducted CUT&RUN-qPCR experiments using immunoprecipitation (IP)-level C/EBPβ antibodies. The results showed that NLRP3 inflammasome activation significantly promoted the binding of C/EBPβ to the Nlrp3 and Il1β gene promoter regions (Figure 4E). However, this effect was inhibited considerably when METTL3 was absent (Figure 4E). To further explore the relationship between METTL3, C/EBPβ, Nlrp3, and Il1β, we generated C/EBPβ-deficient (sh-C/ebpβ) cells and observed that C/EBPβ deficiency significantly inhibited the expression of NLRP3 and pro-IL-1β (Figure 4F). Additionally, we transfected sh-Mettl3 cells with a lentivirus containing the pCDH-C/EBPβ plasmid construct. Through flow cytometry, we selected stable cells that lacked METTL3 but overexpressed C/EBPβ. We found that short hairpin (sh)-Mettl3-pCDH-C/EBPβ cells completely reversed the phenotypes associated with sh-Mettl3 in NLRP3 inflammasome activation (Figure 4G). This reversal included the expression of NLRP3 and pro-IL-1β and the cleavage of GSDMD downstream of the NLRP3 inflammasome (Figure 4G). Moreover, we also observed that the expression of NLRP3, pro-IL-1β, and the cleavage of GSDMD were still induced in sh-Mettl3-Pcdh-C/EBPβ cells without stimulation (Figure 4G). These findings suggest that METTL3 promotes Nlrp3 and Il1β transcription by regulating the transcription factor C/EBPβ.

ce:section.ce:section-title: METTL3 regulates nascent RNA m6A modification during NLRP3 inflammasome activation and activates the JAK1-STAT3-C/EBPβ axis
ce:section.ce:para: Our previous results showed that METTL3 regulates global dynamic transcription during NLRP3 inflammasome activation and promotes Nlrp3 and Il1β transcription in an m6A-dependent manner. However, the exact mechanism of m6A in this process remained unclear. Because METTL3 is the major nuclear methyltransferase responsible for m6A formation, we asked whether it modifies nascent RNAs during inflammasome activation. To address this, we performed chrRNA-MeRIP-seq (Figure 5A). The results showed that NLRP3 inflammasome activation increased m6A levels on both nascent RNAs and non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs) (Figure 5B). In contrast, in METTL3-deficient cells, m6A signals were markedly reduced only on nascent RNAs, not on ncRNAs (Figure 5B). This suggests that inflammation-induced, co-transcriptional m6A modification mainly occurs on RNA polymerase (RNA pol II)-derived nascent transcripts, which are strongly dependent on METTL3. By comparison, many ncRNAs likely originate from RNA pol I/III transcription, where m6A or related modifications are controlled by other methyltransferases. Pathway enrichment analysis revealed that both “inflammasome activation” and “METTL3 loss” affected genes enriched in the JAK-STAT signaling pathway (Figures 5D and 5E). Previous studies have shown that this pathway is a key regulator of C/EBPβ. Consistent with this, we found that inflammasome activation increased m6A modification on nascent Jak1 RNA as well as on Nlrp3 and Il1β transcripts (Figures 5F and 5G–5I). These increases were abolished when METTL3 was deleted (Figures 5G–5I), indicating that METTL3 installs m6A co-transcriptionally on Jak1, Nlrp3, and Il1β nascent RNAs during inflammasome activation.

We next examined how METTL3 affects JAK-STAT signaling. METTL3 loss markedly reduced JAK1 and phosphorylated STAT3 protein levels (Figure 5J). It also decreased p-STAT3 binding to the C/EBPβ promoter (Figure 5K). Nuclear-cytoplasmic fractionation confirmed that nuclear p-STAT3 levels were greatly reduced in METTL3-deficient cells (Figures 5J; S8A), suggesting that STAT3 activation and its transcriptional function were impaired. Similarly, treatment of wild-type cells with the STAT3 inhibitor Stattic reduced p-STAT3 binding to the C/EBPβ promoter and lowered C/ebpβ, Nlrp3, and Il1β mRNA levels (Figures S8B–S8C). These results together indicate that the JAK1-STAT3-C/EBPβ pathway is a key mediator linking METTL3-dependent m6A modification to Nlrp3/Il1β transcription and inflammasome activation. Rescue experiments further confirmed this mechanism. Wild-type METTL3 restored the reduced expression of JAK1, whereas the catalytic mutant D395A did not (Figure 5L). This demonstrates that METTL3’s methyltransferase activity is essential for regulating the JAK1-STAT3-C/EBPβ axis. Finally, analysis of the Jak1 locus showed no changes in chromatin accessibility, nascent RNA production, mRNA expression, or mRNA stability (Figures 5M–5O). However, deletion of JAK1 significantly reduced the expression of C/EBPβ, NLRP3, and pro-IL-1β (Figure 5P).

Taken together, these results demonstrate that METTL3 regulates m6A modification of nascent RNAs during NLRP3 inflammasome activation. By installing m6A on Jak1 transcripts, METTL3 activates the JAK1-STAT3-C/EBPβ-Nlrp3/Il1β signaling axis, thereby promoting inflammasome activation.

ce:section.ce:section-title: METTL3-mediated m6A modifications in nascent RNA enhance the translation of Jak1, Nlrp3, and Il1β mRNA in polysomes
ce:section.ce:para: The results above showed that METTL3 modifies nascent Jak1, Nlrp3, and Il1β RNAs during NLRP3 inflammasome activation. We next asked what these m6A modifications do. METTL3 deletion did not affect Jak1 gene transcription, Jak1 mRNA levels, or Jak1 mRNA stability (Figures 5M–5O). Although METTL3 regulated the transcription of Nlrp3 and Il1β, it also did not change their mRNA half-lives. Therefore, we hypothesized that m6A modification of Jak1, Nlrp3, and Il1β nascent RNAs might enhance translation efficiency rather than mRNA stability. Using the SRAMP online prediction tool, we analyzed the potential m6A peaks on these transcripts. Jak1 showed three high-confidence m6A sites located in the 3′UTR (Figure S9A). Nlrp3 contained two major sites in the coding DNA sequence (CDS) region (Figure S9B), and Il1β had predicted sites in the 3′UTR (Figure S9C). To test the functional role of these sites, we constructed dual-luciferase reporter plasmids containing either wild-type or mutant 3′UTRs of Jak1 and Il1β (Figures 6A and 6B). When transfected into 293T cells, the wild-type 3′UTR reporters of both Jak1 and Il1β showed significantly higher luciferase activity than their mutants (Figures 6A and 6B), suggesting that m6A modification in the 3′UTR promotes translation. Similarly, we generated plasmids encoding the wild-type, single-mutant, and double-mutant CDS regions of Nlrp3 (Figure 6C). In 293T cells, mutation of the m6A site corresponding to the 639-Asp residue markedly reduced NLRP3 protein expression, whereas mutation at 627-Glu had no effect (Figure 6D). These findings indicate that m6A modification in specific regions of Jak1, Nlrp3, and Il1β transcripts facilitates their translation.

YTHDF1 is an m6A reader that promotes translation by recruiting ribosomes to m6A-modified transcripts.31,32 To confirm its involvement, we generated YTHDF1-deficient cells and performed polysome fractionation using sucrose gradient centrifugation (Figure 6E). The overall translation profile was unchanged in METTL3-deficient cells but was markedly reduced in YTHDF1-deficient cells, especially in the heavy polysome fraction (>80S) (Figure 6F). Quantitative reverse-transcription PCR (RT-qPCR) analysis showed that both METTL3 and YTHDF1 deficiency significantly decreased the association of Jak1, Nlrp3, and Il1β mRNAs with heavy polysomes (Figure 6G). To visualize these interactions, we performed RNA-FISH combined with ribosome (18S rRNA) staining. In cells lacking METTL3 or YTHDF1, spatial colocalization of Jak1, Nlrp3, and Il1β mRNAs with ribosomes was markedly reduced (Figure 6H), consistent with polysome profiling. These results suggest that METTL3 promotes ribosome loading through an m6A-YTHDF1-dependent mechanism. At the molecular level, YTHDF1 mainly enhances translation rather than affecting mRNA abundance. Consistent with this, YTHDF1 deletion did not change Jak1 mRNA levels (Figure 6I) but significantly reduced Jak1 mRNA enrichment in polysomes (Figure 6G). Consequently, p-STAT3 activation and C/EBPβ expression were decreased, leading to reduced transcriptional induction of Nlrp3 and Il1β (Figures 6I and 6J). Together, these data support a unified model: during NLRP3 inflammasome activation, METTL3 installs m6A marks co-transcriptionally on nascent Jak1, Nlrp3, and Il1β RNAs. YTHDF1 recognizes these marks and promotes ribosome recruitment. Enhanced translation of Jak1 transcript activates the JAK1-STAT3-C/EBPβ signaling pathway, which drives Nlrp3 and Il1β transcription. In parallel, direct m6A-YTHDF1-mediated translation of Nlrp3 and Il1β further amplifies protein production. Thus, METTL3 and YTHDF1 cooperate to form a feedforward circuit that links m6A-dependent translation with NLRP3 inflammasome activation.

ce:section.ce:section-title: METTL3 ablation in myeloid cells ameliorates acute NLRP3 inflammasome-mediated inflammation
ce:section.ce:para: To evaluate the in vivo effects of METTL3, we generated myeloid-specific knockout mice (Lyz2-Cre-Mettl3f/f). In a sepsis model (Figure 7A), Lyz2-Cre-Mettl3f/f mice showed slightly improved survival compared with littermate controls (Mettl3f/f) (Figure 7B). Serum levels of IL-1β and IL-18 were significantly reduced (Figure 7C). Flow cytometry revealed a shift of splenic macrophages from a proinflammatory M1 phenotype toward an anti-inflammatory M2 phenotype, resulting in a lower M1/M2 ratio (Figure 7D). Histological analysis showed reduced inflammatory cell infiltration in the liver and lungs, as evidenced by and F4/80 immunohistochemistry (Figure 7E). Western blot analysis confirmed decreased activation of inflammasome effector proteins, including GSDMD-N and cleaved IL-1β-p17, in liver and lung tissues (Figure S10A). Moreover, the expression of Nlrp3 and Il1β was reduced in multiple organs, including the liver, lung, spleen, and intestine (Figure S10B). In a sterile acute arthritis model (Figure 7F), Lyz2-Cre-Mettl3f/f mice exhibited reduced joint swelling (Figures 7G and 7H). H&E and F4/80 staining showed fewer infiltrating macrophages in the affected joints (Figure 7I). Caspase-1 activation and NLRP3 expression in joint homogenates were both suppressed (Figure S10C). Together, these findings demonstrate that loss of METTL3 in macrophages effectively attenuates acute NLRP3 inflammasome-mediated inflammation and tissue injury in vivo.

To test whether the downstream pathway is required in vivo, we inhibited STAT3 activity using the selective inhibitor Stattic in wild-type mice. Mice were pretreated with the selective STAT3 inhibitor Stattic and then challenged in the LPS-induced sepsis or MSU-induced arthritis models (Figure S11A). In the LPS-induced sepsis, STAT3 inhibition significantly reduced serum IL-1β and IL-18 levels, suppressed caspase-1 activation and GSDMD cleavage in the liver, and markedly decreased inflammatory cell infiltration (Figures S11B–S11E). In the arthritis (Figure S11F), STAT3 inhibition significantly alleviated ankle swelling and suppressed caspase-1 activation and GSDMD cleavage in the joint (Figure S11H). The phenotypic outcomes of STAT3 inhibition closely resembled those observed in Lyz2-Cre-Mettl3f/f mice, confirming that the JAK1-STAT3-C/EBPβ pathway functions as a key downstream axis of METTL3 signaling. When STAT3 is pharmacologically inhibited, NLRP3 inflammasome activation is strongly suppressed, even when METTL3 remains intact.

ce:section.ce:section-title: METTL3 ablation in myeloid cells prevents diet-induced obesity and protects mice from NLRP3 inflammasome-mediated inflammation
ce:section.ce:para: In recent years, extensive research has focused on the role and mechanism of the NLRP3 inflammasome in obesity and type 2 diabetes (T2D).33,34 IL-1β is recognized as an important contributor to the development of T2D due to its potent inflammatory actions.35,36 In light of this, we aimed to elucidate the specific impact of METTL3 on chronic inflammation in myeloid cells by constructing a mouse model of obesity-related chronic inflammation through a 12-week HFD. Our results are similar to previous reports37 that with Lyz2-Cre-Mettl3f/f mice on a normal diet showed similar body weight gain while also showing resistance to obesity on an HFD diet (Figures 7J and 7K). Moreover, upon HFD, Lyz2-Cre-Mettl3f/f mice displayed reductions in intra-abdominal white adipose tissue and epididymal white adipose tissue parameters, including cell area (Figures S12A–S12D), but did not affect the weight of the liver and brown adipose tissue (Figure S12A). Moreover, Lyz2-Cre-Mettl3f/f mice exhibited improved glucose tolerance and heightened insulin sensitivity (Figures 7L and 7M). These findings were consistently reproduced in female mice through a 14-week HFD (Figures S12E–S12G). Subsequent investigations into blood glucose, triglyceride (TG), and total cholesterol (TC) levels in serum demonstrated significantly reduced blood glucose and TC concentrations (Figure 7N) in Lyz2-Cre-Mettl3f/f mice after HFD feeding, with no notable impact on TG levels (Figure 7N). Considering the established role of caspase-1-mediated IL-1β and IL-18 in promoting T2D development and insulin resistance, we analyzed the protein and gene expression profiles of stromal vascular fraction (SVF) cells (Figures 7O and 7P). Our results indicated a significant decrease in the mature cleavage product of caspase-1 (p10) within the SVF of Lyz2-Cre-Mettl3f/f mice compared to Mettl3f/f mice. In summary, our study sheds light on the intricate interplay of METTL3 in the context of chronic inflammation induced by obesity, elucidating its potential role in attenuating NLRP3 inflammasome-associated metabolic disturbances.

This study reveals an integrated “transcription-translation” model that connects two regulatory layers in macrophages. METTL3 installs m6A marks co-transcriptionally on nascent RNA. On one hand, it acts as a global regulator that reshapes dynamic transcription and chromatin accessibility during NLRP3 inflammasome activation. On the other hand, through m6A-dependent activation of the transcription factor C/EBPβ, it triggers Nlrp3 and Il1β transcription via the JAK1-STAT3-C/EBPβ pathway. Together with YTHDF1, METTL3 further enhances the translation of Nlrp3 and Il1β mRNAs. This “two-layer model” explains the seemingly paradoxical observation of increased chromatin accessibility but reduced local (Nlrp3/Il1β) transcription. It also establishes that transcriptional initiation through the JAK1-STAT3-C/EBPβ axis is the key determinant of Nlrp3/Il1β expression, whereas translation serves as a downstream amplifier.

At the genome-wide level, chrRNA-seq and KAS-seq revealed that NLRP3 activation induces a global repression of nascent transcription and a rearrangement of chromatin accessibility. In this context, loss of METTL3 partially relieved this repression and increased promoter and enhancer accessibility. Differential expression analysis showed that about 37% of genes normally upregulated by inflammasome activation were reversed in METTL3-deficient cells. This proportion mirrors findings in developmental systems: in embryonic stem cells (ESCs) to cardiomyocytes,38 METTL3 knockout reversed ≈63% of downregulated nascent transcripts associated with cardiac-specific genes, indicating that METTL3 shapes large-scale transcriptional patterns rather than regulating a few loci. Importantly, our rescue experiments demonstrated that this global remodeling depends on METTL3’s catalytic activity. Only wild-type METTL3, but not the catalytic mutant D395A, restored nascent RNA synthesis to baseline levels. This m6A-dependent transcriptional regulation parallels observations in ESCs, where METTL3 knockout increases chromatin accessibility and nascent transcription that can be rescued by wild-type but not mutant METTL3. These results are consistent with the “m6A-chrRNA-chromatin” model proposed by Liu et al., in which m6A-marked chrRNAs mediate feedback control of transcription and chromatin state.29 Our findings extend this mechanism from development to inflammation, showing that METTL3 continues to regulate nascent transcription and chromatin remodeling under acute inflammatory stress.

At the gene-specific level, prior studies have demonstrated METTL3’s direct binding to promoter regions,26 influencing gene transcription. However, through CUT&tag-seq experiment, we have identified that METTL3 does not bind to the promoter regions of Nlrp3 and Il1β genes. Instead, we confirm that Nlrp3 and Il1β transcription showed a unique dependence on the JAK1-STAT3-C/EBPβ axis. METTL3 deletion did not affect Jak1 transcription or mRNA stability but reduced Jak1 translation and p-STAT3 levels. Consequently, p-STAT3 binding to the C/EBPβ promoter decreased, leading to lower C/EBPβ expression and impaired Nlrp3/Il1β transcription. Pharmacological inhibition of STAT3 using Stattic mimicked these effects, reducing p-STAT3 occupancy at the C/EBPβ promoter, suppressing C/EBPβ expression, and decreasing Nlrp3/Il1β transcription. Conversely, nuclear fractionation confirmed reduced nuclear p-STAT3 in METTL3-deficient cells. Overexpression of C/EBPβ in METTL3-deficient cells fully restored Nlrp3/Il1β expression and inflammasome activation, demonstrating that the JAK1-STAT3-C/EBPβ axis is the decisive transcriptional switch for Nlrp3/Il1β activation.

At the translational level, our data distinguish mRNA stability from translational efficiency. Actinomycin D chase assays showed no change in Jak1, Il1β, or Nlrp3 mRNA stability. However, polysome profiling and RT-qPCR confirmed that loss of METTL3 or YTHDF1 reduced the enrichment of Jak1, Il1β, and Nlrp3 mRNAs in heavy polysome fractions (>80S). Site-specific mapping by chrRNA-MeRIP-seq and SRAMP prediction identified m6A sites in Jak1 (3′UTR), Il1β (3′UTR), and Nlrp3 (CDS). Dual-luciferase and site-directed mutagenesis experiments showed that mutation of these m6A sites reduced protein expression. RNA-FISH combined with ribosome staining provided spatial confirmation: in METTL3-or YTHDF1-deficient cells, colocalization of these transcripts with ribosomes was significantly reduced. Together, these findings suggest that YTHDF1 recognizes m6A marks and promotes ribosome loading, enhancing translation without altering mRNA stability. Enhanced translation of Jak1 acts as an upstream trigger that activates the JAK1-STAT3-C/EBPβ axis, which initiates Nlrp3 and Il1β transcription. Meanwhile, m6A–YTHDF1–mediated translation of Nlrp3 and Il1β themselves amplifies protein output, forming a positive feedback loop that drives inflammasome activation.

Notably, in our chrRNA-MeRIP-seq analyses, we observed that m6A on nascent RNA is upregulated upon inflammatory stimulation and is sensitive to METTL3 depletion, whereas the total m6A level on ncRNAs does not significantly decrease after loss of METTL3. We view this not as a contradiction to METTL3’s central role but as evidence for a division of labor in m6A deposition across transcriptional systems and substrate classes: under inflammatory conditions, METTL3 likely acts co-transcriptionally on pol II-derived nascent transcripts, while the quantified ncRNA pool is heterogeneous and contains a substantial proportion of pol I/III products whose m6A marks are more plausibly maintained by non-METTL3 pathways (e.g., METTL5, ZCCHC4, and METTL16), yielding a strong effect on nascent RNA but a limited effect on bulk ncRNA.39,40,41 In addition, an assay-level “offset effect” may operate: MeRIP measures aggregate m6A, and METTL3 can alter both the copy number of distinct ncRNA subgroups and the per-molecule m6A occupancy, so countervailing changes across subgroups may cancel at the total level, obscuring subgroup- or site-specific alterations and producing an apparently unchanged global ncRNA m6A signal.

Previous studies linking m6A to NLRP3 inflammasome regulation have focused mainly on post-transcriptional mechanisms, such as mRNA stabilization by METTL14-IGF2BP2.20,23,24 The novelty of this study lies in integrating co-transcriptional m6A modification and chromatin accessibility into the inflammatory signaling framework. We visualize a complete causal chain connecting “METTL3→ chromatin→ nascent RNA→ m6A→ YTHDF1→ enhanced Jak1 translation → STAT3–C/EBPβ activation→ Nlrp3/Il1β transcription→ amplified Nlrp3/Il1β translation,” and demonstrate how METTL3 orchestrates both global transcriptional remodeling and inflammasome-specific gene activation.

From a cellular stress perspective, NLRP3 activation is known to cause K+ efflux, mitochondrial injury, and ROS accumulation, leading to integrated stress response activation (eIF2α phosphorylation and CDK9/Pol II-Ser2P decrease) and caspase-1-mediated cleavage of nuclear substrates such as PARP, DNA-PK, and Lamin A.42,43,44 These events disrupt transcriptional elongation and chromatin structure, representing a “resource redistribution” strategy under stress. Our findings that METTL3 deletion partially alleviates this global transcriptional repression suggest a buffering role of m6A-chrRNA coupling in transcriptional control during inflammation.

At the in vivo level, our results show that myeloid-specific deletion of Mettl3 can significantly alleviate acute inflammation, such as LPS-induced sepsis and MSU-induced arthritis, and improve chronic inflammation and metabolic phenotypes in the HFD model; in wild-type mice, pharmacological inhibition of STAT3 likewise reduces IL-1β/IL-18, suppresses caspase-1 activation and tissue inflammatory infiltration, and joint swelling is concomitantly reduced. These findings are consistent with previous lines of research indicating that inhibiting macrophage JAK-STAT3 signaling can mitigate LPS-induced organ injury/neuroinflammation and that C/EBPβ is associated with inflammatory amplification.45,46,47,48 At the same time, some reports found that myeloid Mettl3 deletion can alleviate obesity and inflammatory progression by remodeling immunometabolism.37,49,50 Compared with these studies, we obtained cross-model, reproducible in vivo evidence across three types of models—acute (sepsis and sterile arthritis) and chronic (obesity-related low-grade inflammation)—thereby strengthening the feasibility and extrapolative value of targeting the Mettl3-STAT3-C/EBPβ axis to modulate NLRP3-driven inflammation.

Overall, the finding that Nlrp3 deletion does not affect global m6A or METTL3/METTL14 levels suggests that m6A acts upstream of inflammasome activation. The “transcriptional drive and translational amplification” model proposed here not only provides a unified explanation for m6A–inflammasome interactions but also offers a potential therapeutic strategy by targeting the METTL3–m6A–YTHDF1–JAK1–STAT3–C/EBPβ axis in inflammation-related diseases.

This study still has several limitations that require systematic reinforcement. First, based on chrRNA-seq, KAS-seq, chrRNA-MeRIP-seq, and WT/MUT-METTL3 rescue, we proposed a directional model—METTL3 → nascent RNA m6A → JAK1-STAT3-C/EBPβ → Nlrp3/Il1β—to explain the epigenetic decoupling whereby chromatin accessibility increases while Nlrp3/Il1β transcription decreases; however, locus-resolved causal evidence is still lacking. Although we extended the framework of chrRNA m6A-mediated feedback on chromatin and transcription29 to macrophage inflammatory activation for the first time, locus-by-locus validation near Nlrp3/Il1β remains necessary. Accordingly, we will combine long-read sequencing to precisely map m6A sites on chrRNAs, perform short-term YTHDC1/NEXT perturbations to assess reader dependence, and integrate KAS-seq, ATAC-seq, H3K27ac, and pol II ChIP-seq, and PRO-seq to readout local accessibility and transcriptional dynamics, while simultaneously monitoring C/EBPβ/p-STAT3 occupancy and Nlrp3/Il1β transcriptional output, thereby upgrading correlation to locus-level causality. Second, the current in vivo evidence for necessity mainly relies on pharmacological STAT3 inhibition, which carries potential off-target and pharmacokinetic limitations; future work should test pathway indispensability in genetic interaction models, including myeloid-specific Stat3/C/ebpβ conditional knockouts combined with Mettl3-cKO. Finally, for translation, the METTL3-nascent m6A-YTHDF1 → JAK1–STAT3–C/EBPβ axis offers multiple intervention nodes (e.g., inhibiting METTL3 or the YTHDF1-m6A interaction, or downstream STAT3), with evaluation of sequential or combination strategies with NLRP3 inhibitors/anti-IL-1 therapy. Priority should be given to myeloid/liver-spleen-enriched delivery and short therapeutic windows to minimize systemic suppression, using IL-1β/IL-18, caspase-1 p20, GSDMD-N, and nuclear p-STAT3 as pharmacodynamic readouts, alongside stratification of populations with high inflammatory burden or metabolic low-grade inflammation, to cautiously advance clinical translation.

Mettl3f/f mice were crossed with Lyz2-cre mice to obtain Lyz2-cre-Mettl3f/f mice. Mice were sex-matched and used at 6–12 weeks of age.
Mice 6–8 weeks old were maintained on an ND or HFD, (60% cal/fat) for 12–14 weeks.

Mice were injected intraperitoneally with LPS. For the sepsis model, mice were sacrificed 6h after the LPS challenge (25 mg/kg), and the serum levels of IL-1β and IL-18 were measured by ELISA. In the survival model, mice were injected with LPS (20 mg/kg) and observed for 60h. For pharmacologic inhibition of STAT3 with Stattic in the LPS model, mice received an intraperitoneal injection of Stattic (10 mg/kg) or PBS 1h prior to LPS challenge.

To induce arthritis, MSU (0.5 mg per mouse) was injected into the joints of mice, and the size of joint was measured at different time points using a digital caliper. For pharmacologic inhibition of STAT3 with Stattic in the MSU model, mice received an injection of Stattic (10 mg/kg) or PBS 1h prior to MSU challenge in the joints.

Briefly, cells were primed with LPS (500 ng/mL) for 4h in Opti-MEM, and followed by stimulation with various NLRP3 inflammasome activators (2.5 mM ATP (30 min); 20 mM nigericin (30 min); 200 mg/mL MSU (5h); 300 mg/mL aluminum salts (5h)). Stattic (5 μM) or PBS was added 2h before LPS treatment. Cell lysates and precipitated supernatants were further analyzed using western blotting and ELISA. All cell lines used in this study, including 293T and J774A.1, and L929, were obtained directly from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC). Cell line identity was authenticated prior to experimental use, and the authentication results matched the reference ATCC profiles. All cell lines were routinely tested for mycoplasma contamination and all tests were negative.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Bone marrow-derived macrophage and peritoneal macrophage isolation
ce:section.ce:para: Bone marrow cells were flushed from femurs/tibias of 6–8-week-old mice, red blood cells (RBCs) were lysed, and cells were differentiated for 7 days in RPMI containing 10% FBS, L-glutamine, 50 μM β-mercaptoethanol, and 40% L929-conditioned medium (prepared by culturing L929 cells 7 days, centrifuging, and 0.45 μm filtering the supernatant). Adherent cells were used as BMDMs.54 Mice received intraperitoneal thioglycolate (Sigma, T0632); 3 days later, the peritoneal cavity was lavaged with PBS. Exudate cells were collected, RBC-lysed, plated, and adherent cells were used as PMs.55

Proteins in culture supernatants were precipitated by the methanol/chloroform method55: mix supernatant with 1 vol methanol and 0.25 vol chloroform, centrifuge (12,000 rpm, 5min) and discard the upper phase. Add 1 vol methanol, mix, centrifuge (5 min), discard supernatant, and air-dry the pellet at 55°C. Resuspend in 60 μL of 2 × loading buffer, boil (100°C, 10 min), and analyze by Western blot.

Cells were lysed in RIPA buffer with protease inhibitors and PMSF. Protein was quantified by BCA (Beyotime P0011), equal amounts were separated by SDS–PAGE, transferred to PVDF, and blocked in 5% non-fat milk for 1h. Membranes were incubated with primary antibodies followed by horseradish peroxidase (HRP)-conjugated secondary antibodies, and signals were detected using ECL (Beyotime P0018S). Total RNA was extracted with TRIzol, reverse-transcribed to cDNA, and amplified using SYBR Green (Roche) on a StepOnePlus real-time PCR system. Gene-specific primers (Table S1; synthesized by Tsingke) were used. The relative mRNA expression of the target gene was analyzed by the 2−ΔΔCT method using the β-actin as a normalization control. Table S2 Specific primers used for real-time PCR.
According to the manufacturer’s protocols, Murine IL-1β and TNF-α cytokines were detected with ELISA kits.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Immunofluorescence staining, tissue histomorphology and immunohistochemical staining
ce:section.ce:para: Immunofluorescence: Cells on glass-bottom dishes were fixed (4% paraformaldehyde, 10 min), washed (PBS ×3), permeabilized (0.1% Triton X-100, 8 min), and blocked (3% BSA, 20 min). Samples were incubated with primary antibody (4°C, overnight), washed, then Alexa Fluor 488 anti-mouse or 594 anti-rabbit secondary (30–45 min, dark). Nuclei were stained with DAPI (1:4000, 5–10 min), mounted with antifade medium, and imaged on a Zeiss LSM710 confocal microscope under identical settings. Histology & IHC (tissues). Mouse tissues were fixed (4% paraformaldehyde, 24h), paraffin-embedded, and sectioned (5 μm). For H&E, sections were stained and imaged (Leica DM3000). For IHC, sections were deparaffinized, rehydrated through graded alcohols, incubated with primary antibody followed by HRP-conjugated secondary, developed, counterstained, and imaged.

SVF was isolated from mouse epididymal fat as described previously.56 Minced tissue was digested in collagenase I (2 mg/mL; 17100017, Gibco) with 3 mM CaCl2 and 2% FBS for 30 min with shaking, filtered through a 40 μm mesh, and centrifuged (1,200 rpm, 5 min). Pellets were treated with pre-cooled red blood cell lysate buffer (5 min), washed, and recentrifuged (1,200 rpm, 5 min).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Glucose tolerance test (GTT) and insulin tolerance test (ITT)
ce:section.ce:para: For GTTs, mice were fasted overnight and injected with D-glucose (2g/kg; 400 mg/mL).57 Blood glucose was measured from the tail vein at 0, 15, 30, 60, 90, and 120 min using a glucometer. For ITTs, after a 5-h fast, mice were injected with recombinant human insulin (0.75 U/kg). Blood glucose levels were measured using a glucometer.57

ce:section.ce:section-title: Serum glucose level and lipid profile analysis
ce:section.ce:para: The serum glucose level and lipid profiles, including TG and TC, were measured with a Hitachi 7600-020 automatic clinical chemistry analyzer (Hitachi).

Single-cell suspensions were prepared by mechanically dissociating spleens and filtering through a 40 μm strainer. Cells were washed with PBS, subjected to RBCs lysis, then resuspended in staining buffer (2% FBS and 1 mM EDTA) and blocked with anti-CD16/32 (15 min, on ice). Surface staining was performed with the indicated antibodies (30 min, on ice, dark). Gating: M1 macrophages, CD45+CD11b+F4/80+CD11c+CD206-; M2 macrophages, CD45+CD11b+F4/80+CD11c−CD206+. Single-stained controls were used for compensation. Data were acquired on a BD LSRFortessa and analyzed with FlowJo.

Cells were treated with actinomycin D (10 mg/mL) and harvested at 0, 3, and 6 h. Total RNA was extracted; an equal amount of RNA spike-in was added to each sample for normalization. After reverse transcription, mRNA levels at each time point were quantified by RT-qPCR.

To evaluate the effect of 3′UTR m6A site on Jak1 and Il1β expression, WT-3′UTR or MUT-3′UTR was inserted downstream of pmirGLO Dual-Luciferase vector. The complete sequence is presented in Table S2. After 48h post-transfection, the activities of firefly luciferase and Renilla luciferase in each 24-well plate’ well were determined by a Dual-Luciferase Reporter Gene Assay Kit according to the product protocol.

As described by Poria et al.58 with minor modifications.56 The sh-Scramble, sh-Ythdf1, and sh-Mettl3 cells were stimulated with LPS+ATP, then treated with cycloheximide (CHX, 100 mg/mL, 10 min, 37°C). Cells were washed 3× with PBS+CHX (100 mg/mL) and pelleted (2,000 g, 5 min). Pellets were lysed in ice-cold buffer (20 mM HEPES, 100 mM KCl, 5 mM MgCl2 and 1% Triton X-100, along with 100 mg/mL CHX, freshly supplemented with a 1:100 protease inhibitor, and 40 U/ml SUPERase RNase Inhibitor) snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen, thawed on ice, and clarified (4°C, 20 min). Supernatants were DNase-treated (Turbo DNase, 15 min); 500 μL lysate was loaded onto freshly prepared 10–50% sucrose gradients (SW41 Ti tubes) and centrifuged (39,000 rpm, 2.5h, 4°C). Fractions were collected with A260 monitoring. RNA from selected fractions was extracted with TRIzol (3× volume) and analyzed by RT-qPCR.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Total RNA-seq library generation, sequencing and analysis
ce:section.ce:para: Total RNA was poly(A)-selected with oligo-dT beads and libraries prepared using NEBNext Ultra II (NEB). Libraries were sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq (PE150). Adapters/low-quality bases were trimmed and reads <36 bp discarded. Clean reads were aligned to mouse mm10 with HISAT2 (v2.0.5); gene counts were generated by featureCounts (v1.5.0-p3) and expression summarized as Fragments Per Kilobase Million (FPKM). Differential expression was performed on raw counts using DESeq2 (v1.20.0) with Benjamini–Hochberg FDR correction.

sh-Scramble and sh-Mettl3 cells were cultured in pre-coated glass over slides. EU markers were added while sh-Scramble and sh-Mettl3 cells were treated with LPS or LPS+ATP. Two hours later, a nascent RNA synthesis assay was conducted using Click EU-488 RNA synthesis Imaging Kits following the manufacturer’s protocols. Images were acquired through a Leica DM3000 Microsystem (Leica, Germany).

Per a published protocol59 (previously established in our lab60) with minor changes. Treated sh-Scramble and sh-Mettl3 cells were washed, scraped, and pelleted (500 g, 2 min, 4°C). Pellets were lysed on ice in cytoplasmic lysis buffer (200μL, 0.15% (vol/vol) NP-40, 10mM Tris-HCl (pH = 7.0), 150mM NaCl, 25μM α-amanitin, 10U SUPERase In and protease inhibitor) layered onto a 25% sucrose cushion (500μL, 10mM Tris-HCl (pH = 7.0), 150mM NaCl, 25% (wt/vol) sucrose, 25μM α-amanitin, 10U SUPERase In and protease inhibitor), and centrifuged (16,000g, 10 min, 4°C) to collect the cytoplasmic fraction (supernatant). The nuclei pellet was washed by 800μL Nuclei wash buffer (0.1%(vol/vol) Triton X-100, 1mM EDTA, PBS, 25μM α-amanitin, 40U SUPERase In and protease inhibitor) and centrifuge at 4°C 1,150g for 1min. After removing the supernatant, the nuclei pellet was resuspended in 200μL Glycerol buffer (20mM Tris-HCl (pH = 8.0), 75mM NaCl, 0.5mM EDTA, 50% (vol/vol) Glycerol, 0.8mM DTT, 25μM α-amanitin, 10U SUPERase In and protease inhibitor), blow and mix well, and transfer the suspension to a new RNase-free 1.5mL centrifuge tube. 200μL Nuclei lysis buffer (1% (vol/vol) NP-40, 20mM HEPES (pH = 7.5), 300mM NaCl, 1M Urea, 0.2mM EDTA, 1mM DTT, 25μM α-amanitin, 10U SUPERase In and protease inhibitor) added, vortex mixed, incubated on ice for 2min, and centrifuged (4°C, 18,500g, 2min) to obtain soluble nucleoplasm fraction and insoluble chromotin-associated fraction. The chromatin was resuspended in a 50μL chromatin resuspension solution (25μM α-amanitin, 10U SUPERase In and protease inhibitor).

Add 700μL of QIAzol lysis reagent to the isolated chromatin, and use a 1mL syringe (22G needle) to slowly blow and mix, so that the insoluble chromatin is wholly broken and dissolved. chrRNA was then isolated using the miRNeasy mini kit. After chrRNA was extracted, rRNAs were removed to retain conding RNAs and ncRNAs. The enriched conding RNAs and ncRNAs were fragmented into short fragments using fragmentation buffers and reverse transcribed into cDNA with random primers. Second-strand cDNA was synthesized by DNA polymerase I, RNase H, dNTP (dUTP instead of dTTP) and buffer. Next, the cDNA fragments were purified with a QiaQuick PCR extraction kit (Qiagen, Venlo, The Netherlands), end repaired, poly(A) added, and ligated to Illumina sequencing adapters. Then UNG (Uracil-N-Glycosylase) was used to digest the second-strand cDNA. The digested products were size selected by agarose gel electrophoresis, PCR amplified, and sequenced using Illumina HiSeqTM 4000 (or other platforms) by Gene Denovo Biotechnology Co. (Guangzhou, China).

chrRNA was isolated from the chromosome-associated fraction of sh-Scramble and sh-Mettl3 cells. Nonribosomal RNA was further enriched from chrRNA and the enriched RNA was fragmented into short fragments (about 100nt) by using a fragmentation buffer. m6A-IP was performed using EpiMark N6-Methyladenosine Enrichment Kit following the manufacturer’s protocols. Library preparation and sequencing were performed on the Illumina sequencing platform by Gene Denovo Biotechnology Co., Ltd (Guangzhou, China).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Quantification of m6A in mRNA and m6A dot blot
ce:section.ce:para: mRNA was purified from total RNA using the GenElute mRNA Miniprep kit (Sigma-Aldrich, MRN70-1KT). mRNA (300 ng) was enzymatically digested (nuclease P1, 2 U, 42°C, 2h; then alkaline phosphatase, 0.5 U, 37°C, 2h) and m6A was quantified by HPLC–QqQ–MS/MS as our previously described.61 The equal amounts mRNA was spotted on nylon membranes, UV-crosslinked (254 nm, 0.12 J/cm2), blocked in PBST +5% milk (1h), incubated with anti-m6A (4°C, overnight), washed (PBST, 3 × 10 min), incubated with HRP-secondary (1h), and developed by ECL; methylene blue staining served as the loading control.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Lentiviral shRNAs and C/EBPβ overexpression lentivirus
ce:section.ce:para: The shRNAs targeting sh-Mettl3, sh-Mettl14, sh-Ythdf1, sh-Nlrp3, sh-C/ebpβ and sh-Jak1 (Table S1) wese cloned into pRSI9-U6-(sh)-UBI-TagrFP-2A-Puro and packaged in Lentix 293T cells. Viral supernatants were collected at 48 h, 0.22 μm-filtered, and used to transduce J774A.1 cell for 24h. Medium was replaced for 24h, then cells were selected with puromycin (2 mg/mL, 2–3 d) and knockdown was verified. The mouse C/EBPβ CDS was subcloned into pCDH-CMV-MCS-EF1-Puro (empty vector as control). Lentivirus was produced by co-transfecting 293T cells with the expression or control vector plus psPAX2 and pMD2.G using Lipofectamine 3000, and used to transduce target cells.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Construction of NLRP3 CDS mutant plasmid
ce:section.ce:para: The full-length cDNA sequence of mouse Nlrp3 gene was synthesized with a Myc tag at the N terminus and cloned into pCMV-Myc-N expression plasmid to generate the wild-type construct (NLRP3-WT). Nucleotide 890 of the Nlrp3 CDS sequence was mutated (5′-GAACU-3′ to 5′- GAGCU-3′) to generate the mutant-type construct (NLRP3-Mut-Glu-627). Nucleotide 939 of the Nlrp3 CDS sequence was mutated (5′-AGACU-3′ to 5′- GAGTU-3′) to generate the mutant-type construct (NLRP3-Mut-Asp-639). Nucleotides 890 and 939 of the Nlrp3 CDS sequence were mutated (5′-GAACU-3′ to 5′- GAGCU-3’; 5′-AGACU-3′ to 5′- GAGTU-3′) to generate the mutant-type construct (NLRP3-Mut-Glu-627+Mut-Asp-639). The complete sequence is presented in Table S4.

ce:section.ce:section-title: CUT&Tag library generation, sequencing and analysis
ce:section.ce:para: CUT&Tag was performed with the Hyperactive In-Situ ChIP Library Prep Kit (Vazyme, TD901) with minor adaptations.62 Cells were transferred to low-bind 1.5 mL tubes, mixed with 10 μL pre-washed ConA beads (Vazyme N411), and incubated 10 min, RT. Bead-bound cells were incubated in 50 μL Antibody Buffer containing 1 μg anti-METTL3 2h, RT, then washed 2× with 800 μL Digi-wash buffer. A 1 μg secondary antibody in 50 μL Digi-wash was added (45 min), followed by 2 × 800 μL Digi-wash. Next, 100 μL Digi-300 buffer plus 0.58 μL pG-Tn5 was added (1h), samples were washed 2× with Digi-wash, then tagmented in 300 μL Tagmentation Buffer (37°C, 1h). Reactions were stopped by adding 10 μL 0.5 M EDTA +3 μL 10% SDS +2.5 μL Proteinase K (20 mg/mL) and incubating 37°C, 1h. DNA was purified by phenol:chloroform extraction, ethanol-precipitated, air-dried, and resuspended in 25 μL TE. Libraries were PCR-amplified (Vazyme TD204) and sequenced on Illumina HiSeq X Ten/2500 per manufacturer instructions. Raw reads were trimmed with Trimmomatic-0.39 and then mapped to mouse genome (mm10) using bowtie2 (version 2.4.1) with “—dovetail” parameter in default mode: search for the multiple alignments, report the best one. Duplicated reads were removed with samtools “rmdup”. Peaks were called using HOMER in factor style with “-F 2 -L 2 -tagThreshold 10” parameters. Peaks identified in two biological replicates were pooled using bedtools (v.2.26.0) and were used in further analysis. The ENCODE blacklist was downloaded and used to mark CUT&RUN peaks. ROSE identified peaks with high intensity with default parameters.

The cells were processed using the Hyperactive pG-MNase CUT&RUN Assay Kit (Vazyme, HD101-01). Cells were bound to ConA-coated magnetic beads, permeabilized with digitonin, incubated with anti-p-STAT3 or anti-C/EBPβ, and subjected to pAG-MNase digestion/release. DNA was purified (FastPure gDNA Mini Columns) and quantified by PCR/qPCR using primers listed in Table S5.

KAS-seq libraries were generated according to a previous protocol.63 Cells were pulse-labeled in pre-warmed medium with 5 mM N3-kethoxal (10 min, 37°C, 5% CO2), collected, and genomic DNA (gDNA) was purified by PureLink genomic DNA mini kit (Thermo, K182002). gDNA (1 μg) was click-conjugated with DBCO-PEG4-biotin (DMSO solution, Sigma, 760749) in 25 mM potassium borate buffer (37°C, 1.5h), treated with RNase A (Thermo, 12091039) (37°C, 5 min), and cleaned up. Biotinylated gDNA was then recovered by DNA Clean & Concentrator-5kit (Zymo, D4013). DNA was tagmented; 5% was kept as input and the remaining 95% was enriched on streptavidin beads (15 min), washed, PCR-amplified, and purified (MinElute PCR purification kit, Qiagen 28804). Libraries were sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 (PE150), targeting ∼30 million reads per library.

Low quality and adapter containing reads were trimmed from KAS-seq raw data using trim-galore package. Reads shorter than 80bp were removed. Trimmed reads were aligned to the reference genome (mm10) using bowtie2 (v2.3.3.1) under default parameters. Mapped sam files were subsequently converted and sorted to bam files using samtools sort (v1.9). Duplicates were removed using samtools rmdup (v1.9) to get the unique mapped reads. Bam files were converted to bed files and bedGraph files using bedtools. BedGraph files were then converted to bigWig files using bedgraphtobigwig. Peaks were called using MACS2 (v2.2.7.1) with using broad peaks-call mode under default parameters, except for ‘--broad-cutoff = 0.05’. FDR cut-off of 0.05 was used to determine significant peaks. The ChIPseeker R package was invoked to annotate nearest genes and genomic features to peaks. Differentially peaks were identified by DiffBind with a cut-off value of log2|fold change|>0 and p value < 0.05. The clusterProfiler was used to perform functional enrichment analysis for the annotated significant peaks based on Gene Ontology (GO) and the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG). HOMER(v4.11) was utilized to search for sequence motif among significant peaks. E value cutoff of 0.05 was used to select significantly enriched motifs.

RNA-FISH probes targeting Jak1, Nlrp3, Il1β and 18S were custom-designed and synthesized by GenePharma Technology Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China). Cells in a confocal dish were cultured to ∼50–70% confluence; the medium was removed, cells were rinsed with PBS, fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde at room temperature for 15 min, rinsed with PBS, and permeabilized with 0.1% Triton X-100 for 15 min; samples were pre-equilibrated in 2× SSC at 37°C for 30 min. Fluorescent probes were prepared in hybridization buffer (final 1–2 μM), denatured at 73°C for 5 min and immediately applied to the cells, followed by overnight hybridization at 37°C in a humidified, dark chamber. The next day, cells were washed at 42°C sequentially with 0.1% Tween 20/4× SSC, 2× SSC, and 1× SSC for 5 min each; stained with DAPI for 10 min, rinsed with PBS. Images were acquired on a confocal microscope under identical acquisition settings and quantitatively analyzed.
The statistical analyses were done as described in the figure legend with the GraphPad Prism software.
